article.title: Groundwork and the Limits of Left Pragmatism
article.content: R&R member Nikoli Weir writes on the political contradictions of Groundwork, rooted in the influence of bourgeois pragmatism. Signed articles do not necessarily represent the collective views of Reform & Revolution. The socialist left is in crisis. It has, for the past several decades, failed to provide a serious alternative to the current state of affairs. It has produced mountains of criticism of the present state of things, much of which is necessary and correct in its challenge to the dominant worldview, but which does not provide a program and strategy for our political moment. It is composed in large part by isolated, high-control sects that act more like guardians of the faith than a mass political formation. In response to the impotence of much of the organized left, there has emerged a bold, anti-tradition futurism which professes to go beyond the stale formulas of the representatives of revolutionary tradition. More often than not, it ends up falling into unprincipled opportunism. As the socialist movement expands and contracts, it tends to fluctuate between these two poles: uninspiring reliance on tradition on the one hand, and a “new, pragmatic” opportunism on the other. The result is that at any given time, the socialist left is held hostage by each of its two caricatures. “Pragmatism”, in this context, refers to a political framework that prioritizes working within currently existing political structures, not for the purpose of transforming or undermining them, but because doing so appears to be taking the path of least resistance, the path that “works” more than the others. There are endless examples of the former, missionary-style model from all over the Marxist political spectrum, ranging from the far-flung fragments of Trotskyism to the various Stalinist and Maoist organizations. In the United States, organizations like the People’s Defense Committee (PDC) seek to build dual power at the workplace and neighborhood level which can then serve as the basis for a new revolutionary social order. Their primary form of political activity, however, is the same charity work conducted by any number of churches or local Food Not Bombs groups. Examples of the latter, amorphous tendency are harder to pin down, in considerable part due to the content of their politics. They can take an ultra-left or reformist form depending on circumstance. This back-and-forth tendency exists most clearly within the Democratic Socialists of America. This is in part due to the structure of DSA itself, which encourages the formation of factions and caucuses based on common political interests among members. This is a good thing, as it allows these tendencies to be discussed in an environment of free and fair debate connected to mass organizing. Let’s examine a tendency that, in my view, perfectly demonstrates the pseudo-innovative opportunism characteristic of the “pragmatic” tendency in socialist politics. I will, in a later article, address sectarianism, but next time instead of analyzing a caucus, we will talk about a specific DSA chapter. Out of all of the currently active tendencies in DSA, the Groundwork Caucus most exemplifies the opportunist and vacillating tendency within the American Marxist left. Unlike many other DSA caucuses which either emerged out of a pre-existing political tradition (Bread and Roses, Reform and Revolution, Liberation, etc), Groundwork belongs to another category of those which seek to establish their own tendency and tradition, alongside Marxist Unity Group and Mountain Caucus. Groundwork is particularly eclectic in contrast to MUG’s interest in the Second International’s revolutionary period and Mountain’s Gramscianism. The “Groundwork Thought” library brings together Hal Draper, Ralph Milliband, Geese magazine, Fidel Castro, and more. This theoretical amorphism is carried directly into Groundwork’s practical work. Take, for example, Groundwork’s position on the leadership of the labor movement, which they spell out in their 2026 “Tasks and Perspectives” document. Groundwork embraces “working with union leadership when it advances the socialist project, and contesting for power within union leadership when it does not.” Groundwork claims that “union leadership…is deeply heterogeneous—with some leaders closely aligned with our goals, others fiercely opposed, and still others in between.” They go on to say that the socialist movement should “consider collaborating with leadership where we believe working together will help build longer-term class alignment and achieve our short-to-medium term goals, and consider organizing to replace that leadership in unions that actively obstruct the socialist project.” It goes without saying that our attitude towards and willingness to work with the leadership of unions should be determined by whether or not doing so will advance the cause of socialism. However, what needs to be answered before we can answer the question of working with union leadership is the following; what is the position of the leadership in the class struggle between workers and capitalists? Do union leaders and bureaucrats have more in common with the workers in their unions, or with the bosses who they are supposed to be fighting against? Furthermore, we must ask whether the things held in common are primarily ideological, organizational, or class interests. Though the existing union bureaucracy and its leaders are not themselves capitalists, their immediate interests often align more with the capitalists and their managerial servants than they do with the workers that they are supposed to represent. Union leaders, like managers and foremen, are separated from the production process. Both make significantly more money than the workers below them. And most importantly, both more often than not share an interest in preserving the status quo, as their social position depends on the stable flow of dues. The capitalists tolerate the little influence that the labor bureaucrats have in the workplace and wider society because the labor bureaucrats have historically stifled the workers’ movement by suppressing union democracy and opposing attempts to introduce class-struggle politics onto the shop floor. International Brotherhood of Teamsters president Sean O’Brien speaking at the 2024 Republican National Convention. (Photo: Will Lanzoni/CNN) Because the social position of the bureaucracy depends on the continued existence of the union, it is contradictory in character and can sometimes be compelled to act in defense of working-class interests. As a result, there exists a reformist or “left” wing of the bureaucracy, exemplified by United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain and many local labor leaders, who support democratic reforms such as open bargaining and are often friendly to socialists. While socialists can and should work with these figures on a united-front basis, relying on them can render socialists and union militants dependent on their whims. This dependence will inevitably undermine the struggle for democracy and socialism by placing the left on the side of the “progressive” apparatus against the rank-and-file. There are also those within the bureaucracy who use the language of militancy and class independence for cynical and reactionary purposes, such as Sean O’Brien of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Though Groundwork is correct in saying that the views of the labor leadership are heterogeneous, it fails to see that it is not about the orientation of this or that leader; it is about the class relations that the labor bureaucrats exist within, which create structures that incentivize them to act against the interests of the workers that they are supposed to represent. The fact that Teamsters for a Democratic Union, one of the most longstanding and influential union reform caucuses, still supports O’Brien after his open support for Trumpism is a powerful warning against illusions in left-talking bureaucrats. It seems that Groundwork’s hedged position exists solely to justify the caucus’s wavering on the question of the labor bureaucracy. This indecisiveness is present in their electoral strategy just as much as their views on union work. In the same “Tasks and Perspectives” document, Groundwork lays out two different approaches to electoral activity in DSA. On one end, you have the “left” approach, which seeks to use elections and elected offices as primarily bully pulpits to agitate and organize the working class. On the other end, elected office is fundamentally seen as a way to pass reforms that would improve the immediate quality of life for the working class. Under this model, according to Groundwork, candidates are “given leeway to operate independently coordinated DSA strategy, and sometimes even excused for taking stands that run counter to the will of the organization.” So, which of these two contradictory approaches is correct, according to Groundwork? Both! We contend that both of these approaches to electoral work get something right and something wrong, and that the best path forward entails a productive synthesis of these positions. Our strategy for building socialism entails winning and wielding state power to pass transformative reforms; as such, we reject the idea of running candidates to agitate and politicize rather than to win. At the same time, we believe candidates and socialists in office should work within a coordinated strategy set democratically by DSA members at the local, regional and national level, and that our races should popularize socialism and build the organization. Immediately we see that Groundwork’s electoral position is structured in the exact same way as their position on labor. At first glance, it appears very close to Reform & Revolution’s position on the role of struggles for immediate economic and democratic demands in rebuilding a mass socialist movement. However, once you look at Groundwork’s actual role within electoral work in DSA, it becomes clear that their position is reformist in character. Groundwork’s “middle-ground” position is reflective of the destructive influence of pragmatism in the socialist movement. For evidence of this, look no further than Groundwork’s position on whether or not NYC-DSA should have re-endorsed AOC for Congress in the midterm elections. AOC has for multiple years consistently betrayed the movement and organization that she claims to champion. She has run cover for the Biden Administration’s horrendous lies about “working towards a ceasefire in Gaza”; she has voted consistently to continue funding Israel’s “Iron Dome” missile defense system, which provides literal cover for Israel to terrorize the Middle East with no fear of serious retaliation; in 2022, under the Biden Administration, she voted to break the then ongoing rail strike, which constituted one of the largest such strikes in decades. Not only that, but this vote went directly against DSA’s stated position, and she was admonished by name by the National Political Committee, who said as follows: “We disagree and are disappointed with the decision of DSA members Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and and Rep. Cori Bush to needlessly vote to enforce the [tentative agreement]… the members are the union and a majority of members voted to reject the [tentative agreement]. Socialist electeds must stand with unions when they reject a [tentative agreement].” With all of this in mind, it seems clear that, based on their principles, Groundwork should have been against re-endorsing AOC. However, their actual position is just the opposite. In an article titled “The Case for NYC-DSA Endorsing AOC in 2026” , Groundwork openly acknowledges all of AOC’s offenses against both DSA and her constituents. Despite that, they maintain that “AOC is our best chance to achieve an arms embargo against Israel.” They argue that in 2028, the likely Democratic frontrunners will be Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom, and AOC. Out of those three options, they argue that AOC is the most likely person to implement an arms embargo against Israel, and that if we want to give her campaign as much steam as possible, that we should ensure she is re-elected to the House of Representatives in the mid term elections. This is despite the fact she has gone back on her word multiple times, and despite the fact that she isn’t a cadre candidate, both of which are acknowledged by Groundwork. In spite of this, they supported a congressional re-endorsement for AOC on the basis that not doing so would “damage [our] relationship, and would likely shut the door for a national DSA endorsement for 2028.” Unlike much of the DSA “left,” Reform & Revolution recognizes that we cannot simply will an independent left presidential campaign into existence. We recognize, with Groundwork, that AOC is (at this point in time) the only plausible left-labor candidate for the 2028 elections. This is where our agreement with Groundwork reaches its limits. For R&R, DSA’s involvement in AOC’s campaign should primarily be about DSA, not AOC. We should use the AOC campaign to organize people into DSA, advocate for and spread our views and our program, and build up a strong working-class political formation that can effectively outweigh the opportunism of AOC, which she will inevitably bring with her into the Oval Office. DSA’s intervention in a future AOC presidential run isn’t about “access” to power, it’s about how we can use the levers of mass political engagement to build power. At the end of the day, the fundamental difference is if such a campaign is run for AOC’s sake, or for DSA’s. Groundwork uses the language of pragmatism to claim that they are in fact in favor of running class-struggle campaigns, while also running campaigns on a limited, reformist basis. But where are these “class-struggle campaigns” that Groundwork believes are so important to the movement? Why is it that, when push comes to shove, Groundwork always prioritizes the reformist and opportunist approach over the class-struggle approach? Why is it that DSA’s “coordinated strategy,” to use Groundwork’s own words, is also sacrificed for the sake of reformism and opportunism? It is quite simple. The class-struggle approach to electoralism is sacrificed for the reformist approach, because that is the point of the vagueness of Groundwork’s position. This “pragmatic” approach allows Groundwork to claim to support bold, independent tactics in instances where doing so “works,” while never actually doing so, under the guise of there being no plausible class-struggle campaigns to wage. Because the class-struggle path is seemingly “unworkable,” it allows Groundwork to always put it off into the future. Not this campaign, but the next one! We aren’t ready now, but soon we will be! And the moment we are ready, we will do what needs to be done. That moment naturally never comes, so Groundwork continues doing what they always do. This is opportunism par excellence , and it can be seen in every one of Groundwork’s major positions. Not only that, but this can be seen whenever opportunism is the dominant approach to politics, whether it be in the German Social Democrats in the 20s, the Communist Party USA in the 30s, or today’s reformists in DSA. Groundwork’s opportunism can be explained within the framework of the Triple Crisis and Dual Task. Traditionally, Trotskyists have maintained that the crisis of our age is a crisis of leadership; that is, the working class movement is failing to meet the moment because its leadership in the political parties and the trade unions is opportunist, reformist, or deficient in some other way. Because of this emphasis, Trotskyists have historically focused on building up revolutionary cores within mass movements, revolutionary cores who work patiently to win the mantle of leadership away from the bourgeois reformists and labor bureaucrats and lead the workers to victory in the battle for democracy. Though R&R continues to recognize the crisis of leadership as playing a central role in our organizing work, we expand it to include two other crises; the crisis of organization and the crisis of consciousness. The truth of the matter is that the conditions of the 21st century are radically different from the conditions in which Trotsky first laid out the crisis of leadership. The 1930s were a period where the working-class movement was much more developed politically and organizationally, a time of mass parties and mass struggles; it was, theoretically, possible for a small core of revolutionaries to make qualitative leaps toward mass influence in a short period of time. Right now, the situation is very different. The working-class parties and organizations formed in the early and mid 20th century have been neutered and destroyed by decades of austerity and counter-insurgency. The working class as a political subject has spent years in disarray, often not even recognizing itself as a class with class-specific interests and goals. Union membership in the United States has been at an all time low for a long time, and the sphere of mass organization necessary to scaffold a political project, to foster a class worldview and class social bonds, is extremely weak. In the past few years genuine progress has been made. Promising new unions have cropped up in industries that have historically been unorganized, like Starbucks Workers United and the Amazon Labor Union. DSA, which is by a large margin the only relevant socialist organization in the US doing national work, can boast some major wins, such as electing its candidate to the New York City Mayor’s office and breaching 130,000 members. However, despite these successes, the crises of leadership, organization and consciousness remain. If any progress is to be made in surmounting these strategic problems, then we must address them simultaneously. The crises are dialectically interrelated with each other, and any attempt to address one without addressing the others will kneecap the movement. It is this that is the source of Groundwork’s errors. Groundwork focuses exclusively on resolving the crisis of organization, choosing to rely on an amorphous political pragmatism, a “whatever works, works” approach to party-building. This pragmatism does not interrogate what it means for something to “work,” or who and what it is working for. It assumes that anything that builds DSA numerically is good. This results in them having a strong base of active members who are able and willing to participate in the struggles of the day, but who often have difficulty correctly analyzing the problems that caused the crisis and chartering plausible paths forward. This in part explains Groundwork’s theoretical confusion, which we have already discussed. Of course a caucus that prioritizes the development of DSA’s immediate organizational capacity above all other considerations will end up adopting confused, contradictory positions. The confusion and contradiction are not errors; they are on purpose. A position that is in reality a non-position, that can go whichever way the wind blows, serves Groundwork perfectly. It allows them to hold radical principles in theory, while in reality giving them leeway to subordinate their principles for the sake of growing DSA. Here we get to the key point: you cannot meaningfully and effectively grow an organization like DSA by sacrificing its long-term aims and principles for short-term publicity and influence. This will backfire, every time. DSA as an organization does not exist to serve itself. It exists to advance the cause, aims and principles of socialism. Without those principles and ideas, and without an independent working-class political base, DSA means nothing. We could, right now, sacrifice all of our principles, totally cave to the establishment Democrats, and go all in on becoming an organ of the Democratic Party. If we did this, it is likely that we could get quite a few paper members elected to local and state legislatures all across the country, and maybe even build a large socialist bloc in Congress. But would it be worth it? Would it really be a win for DSA if in order to achieve this we had to sacrifice everything that makes DSA what it is? One suspects that Groundwork knows the answer is “no.” It is very possible that Groundwork’s approach “works,” if by “works” we mean succeeds in gaining recognition and members for DSA. But what then? For what purpose does Groundwork wish to build DSA? For what purpose does Groundwork seek to elect socialists to office? These are not ends in themselves. They are means to the end of the socialist transformation of society. If we elect members to all levels of government, but they do nothing more than trail the “progressive” Democrats, we may as well have not elected them at all. If we recruit thousands of members, only to funnel them into doorknocking campaigns for “socialists” who are reluctant to even declare themselves as such, and who are nearly indistinguishable from progressive liberals like Brad Lander, we might as well have not recruited them at all. Our end goal isn’t to endlessly elect socialists into office. Our goal is to transform American society by means of a mass socialist movement. To that end, we run DSA candidates in elections, with the understanding that bourgeois elections are a means to spread our message, advance transitional demands and structural reforms, and use elected office as a bully pulpit to organize the masses. The moment we confuse the means with the ends is the moment that we cease to be a fighting organization of the working class whose aim is the total transformation of society, and become a social-humanitarian group whose highest aspiration is the passing of ultimately inadequate reforms that do nothing to address the root cause of our social ills.
